summary: Introduces a 6to4 anycast address so 6to4 routers can find relays without manual setup, and defines how relays use it and advertise its prefix. It also records IANA's reservation. This document is historic and was replaced by RFC 7526.

plainLanguage.summary: Small networks using 6to4, a way to carry IPv6 traffic inside IPv4, need a helper router called a relay to reach the real IPv6 Internet, and configuring one by hand was hard and often slow. RFC 3068 gives all relays one shared address, so ordinary routing delivers each packet to the nearest relay automatically. The RFC is now Historic, replaced by RFC 7526.

questions: how do 6to4 routers find a relay
subtitle: One well-known IPv4 prefix that lets a 6to4 router find the nearest relay to the IPv6 Internet.

tldr.problem: A small 6to4 network needs a default IPv6 route pointing at a relay router to reach the native IPv6 Internet, but finding one is a significant hurdle, and a route found by hand often points to a router on the far side of the Internet with very poor performance.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reserves the IPv4 prefix 192.88.99.0/24 for 6to4 relay routers to advertise. A 6to4 router sends its IPv6 default route to the matching anycast address, and normal IPv4 routing delivers the packets to the nearest advertising relay.
tldr.outcome: The document is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 7526; it also records IANA's reservation of the prefix.

today: RFC 3068 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 7526. The anycast prefix it defined is no longer the current specification for finding 6to4 relays.

sections.title: The Default Route Problem
sections.content:
RFC 3056 defines 6to4, and gives a 6to4 routing domain two deployment options. If the domain runs an IPv6 exterior routing protocol, its routers learn routes to all existing IPv6 networks through the combination of exterior and interior routing. If not, each 6to4 router using a given relay router needs a default IPv6 route pointing at that relay.

The second case is the typical one for small networks, and the RFC says that finding and configuring the default route is in practice a significant hurdle. Even when managers find a route, it often points to a router on the other side of the Internet, leading to very poor performance.

This memo proposes a standard method to define the default route. 6to4 packets sent to it are routed automatically to the nearest available relay router. The scheme also lets relay managers control which sources may use their relays, and makes it easy to set up many relays so the service can scale.

The RFC is candid about anycast's operational cost: because the sending router does not learn which specific relay received its packets, a transient or intermittent failure is hard to pin on one device. Anycast solutions must therefore include monitoring of the service routers and fault isolation procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Small 6to4 networks had to be told by hand which helper router to use, and the helper they found was often very far away. This memo gives every helper one shared address, so ordinary routing picks a nearby one.

sections.title: The Anycast Prefix and Related Addresses
sections.content:
The memo keeps the RFC 3056 definitions of a 6to4 router, an IPv6 router supporting a 6to4 pseudo-interface and normally sitting between an IPv6 site and a wide-area IPv4 network, and a 6to4 Relay Router, a 6to4 router configured to support transit routing between 6to4 and native IPv6 addresses. It adds four definitions of its own.

The 6to4 Relay anycast prefix is the IPv4 prefix 192.88.99.0/24, used to advertise an IPv4 route to an available relay. The 6to4 Relay anycast address is host number 1 in that prefix, 192.88.99.1. The 6to4 IPv6 relay anycast address is what those values become through the 6to4 mapping rules with a null prefix and null host identifier: 2002:c058:6301::.

The fourth term, the Equivalent IPv4 unicast address, is a regular IPv4 address belonging to one specific relay. Packets sent to it are treated by that relay exactly as packets sent to the anycast address would be, which lets an operator address and test a single relay.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo defines one shared IPv4 block, one shared IPv4 address inside it, the matching IPv6 address, and a private address for each relay so that one relay can be checked on its own.

sections.title: How Routers and Relays Behave
sections.content:
On the site side, a 6to4 router is configured with the default IPv6 route ::/0 pointing to the 6to4 IPv6 anycast address. Packets matching that route are encapsulated in IPv4, with the 6to4 router's own IPv4 address as source and the IPv4 address extracted from the anycast route as destination.

On the relay side, a relay following this memo advertises the 6to4 anycast prefix using the interior gateway protocol of its IPv4 autonomous system, as if it were a connection to an external network. It then receives the packets bound to the anycast address and relays them to the IPv6 Internet as RFC 3056 specifies. Each advertising relay MUST also provide an equivalent IPv4 unicast address, which is processed the same way as the anycast address.

To serve neighbouring autonomous systems, the managers advertise reachability of the prefix with the exterior gateway protocol. When that advertisement uses BGP, the initial AS path must contain the announcing AS's number, and the RFC suggests recording the router's equivalent IPv4 address in the BGP aggregator attribute, while noting that further work is needed on that point. To IPv4, the whole IPv6 network then appears as a single multi-homed network with access points scattered across the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Site routers send everything for the IPv6 Internet to the shared address. Each relay announces the shared prefix inside its own network and, if it wishes, to its neighbours. IPv4 routing then carries the packets to whichever relay is nearest.

sections.title: Monitoring, Failover, Access Control and Scale
sections.content:
Every relay implementing the memo must include a monitoring function that checks the relay function is working, and must stop injecting the anycast route immediately when it is not. The local interior gateway protocol then computes a route to the next best relay, so traffic fails over automatically.

The equivalent IPv4 address supports both monitoring and fault isolation. An operator can test a relay remotely by tunneling a test IPv6 packet through its equivalent address, can build a centralized monitoring function from the list of equivalent addresses, and, when a user reports a problem, can first retrieve the equivalent address of the router that user reached, from interior routing tables or from exterior data such as BGP path attributes, then run connectivity tests against it.

Access control follows the business structure: only autonomous systems that run relays and are willing to serve the IPv6 network announce the prefix, and they can use existing peering and transit agreements to decide who may use the service, and possibly to charge for it.

The RFC also answers questions raised in the NGTRANS working group. On scale: a few relays can carry early 6to4 traffic, and more ISPs can add relays as demand grows, with standard IPv4 routing always directing traffic to the nearest one. On prefix size: a single address, a /32, would be carried in theory, but in practice default-free networks filter routes that are too specific, for example refusing anything smaller than a /24, so the /24 exists to survive those filters, even if it spends some addressing resource in the cause of moving to IPv6. On the transition: the RFC argues the scheme eases the move out of tunnelling, because easy connectivity to the real IPv6 network builds trust in taking a real IPv6 address. An early idea of a dedicated AS number for all relays proved unnecessary for practical operation.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay that breaks must withdraw its announcement so traffic moves to the next one. Each relay's private address lets operators test it and track down faults. Only willing networks announce the service, using their existing business agreements to control access. The author also defends the design against worries about address waste and delayed migration.

sections.title: Security, Future Work and IANA
sections.content:
The security section is short. The generic risks of 6to4 tunnelling and their protections are covered in RFC 3056. The anycast technique adds one risk of its own: a rogue router or a rogue autonomous system could inject a bogus route to the 6to4 anycast prefix and thereby divert the traffic. IPv4 network managers must guarantee the integrity of routing to this prefix in much the same way they guarantee the integrity of their IPv4 routing generally.

As future work the RFC flags one drawback of default routes: the chosen relay may not lie on the most direct path to the target IPv6 address, and in early deployment the nearest relay may be some third party's relay with poor connectivity. A possible remedy, left for further study, is a redirection procedure by which the 6to4 router learns the most appropriate route for a specific destination. Practical operation will also need monitoring and testing tools and gradual management practices, guided by deployment experience.

On IANA, the memo documents the allocation of the IPv4 prefix dedicated to 6to4 gateways to the native IPv6 Internet; no recurring assignment is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake announcement of the shared prefix could divert traffic, so managers must protect routing as they do for IPv4. The nearest relay is not always the best one; a redirection scheme was left for later. IANA's role was to record the one-off prefix allocation.
